We present a tensor-network method that chooses no subsystems and whose memory and run time per solve are set by the number of modes and two truncations, the Fock cutoff of each normal mode and the bond dimension of a matrix product state (MPS), not by the Hilbert-space dimension. From the capacitance matrix, the inverse-inductance matrix and the junction list alone, the linear circuit is diagonalized into normal modes. Each junction cosine is then a sum of two products of single-mode operators, so the complete lumped-element Hamiltonian is a matrix product operator (MPO) of small bond dimension with one site per mode, solved by the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). The normal modes make the method generic, and the tensor network makes it affordable. For two fluxonia joined by a tunable coupler, the method agrees with exact diagonalization of the same truncated space to within 1 MHz. Our circuit of three fluxonia joined by two couplers has 11 normal modes and a truncated space of $10^9$ states, out of reach of exact diagonalization in dense or sparse storage. At a bond dimension of 32, its lowest eight levels are converged to within 1 MHz in both truncations, and each state is stored in a small fraction of the numbers a dense vector needs. One solve at that bond dimension takes 81 min and 1.3 GB of memory on one CPU node.

title: Efficient training of a 128-modes 3D continuously coupled photonic chip via limited quantum resources
summary: Integrated photonics provides a promising route towards the development of large-scale, stable and low-loss quantum hardware. Existing implementations of universal quantum photonic chips generally rely on architectures consisting of localised interactions between the modes that can be programmed with known algorithms to implement specific operations. Recent advances have shown that interferometers based on 3D continuously coupled waveguide arrays may allow to significantly scale up the number of modes with reduced overhead. However, for this class of devices, optimal strategies to set the controllable parameters and obtain the desired transformation have not been demonstrated generally. In this work, we report the use of a machine learning algorithm driven by quantum data to program the operation of a reconfigurable three-dimensional continuously coupled photonic device comprising 128 modes. We show experimentally the capability of reaching a target unitary matrix, among those achievable by the device, through a limited number of one- and two-photon measurements. Our results demonstrate that this approach results to be effective in the presence of noise and with a limited amount of resources, also allowing to partially compensate imperfections in the experimental setup. This method can thus represent a viable route towards programming large scale integrated photonic devices, unlocking the possibility of controlling photonic systems for which an analytical decomposition is not trivial.

title: Trinetra.Q: Statistical and Behavioral Detection of Attacks on the Quantum-Error-Correction Layer and Classical Control Stack of Quantum Computing Systems
summary: Most quantum-computer security work targets physical-layer attacks on qubits, while two surfaces remain inadequately defended: the quantum-error-correction (QEC) syndrome-and-decoder pipeline, and the classical control and software stack that runs it. Tampering on these surfaces can corrupt a computation while the physical error rate appears normal, and can stay within a single-circuit integrity tolerance. We present Trinetra.Q, a detection layer of cooperating detectors, each monitoring a statistical or behavioral property of quantum-domain data against an envelope calibrated from honest operation, and raising an indication only on a statistically significant deviation. The detectors cover (A) QEC integrity over per-stabilizer firing rates, syndrome defect-count, and repeated-syndrome rate; (B) decoder confidence over the margin between minimum-weight error explanations in distinct logical classes; (C) behavioral output divergence, flagging crosstalk-class and novel attacks by their effect on a victim's output relative to a matched control; (D) control-stack tampering via known-answer canary circuits, built to be indistinguishable to a resident implant, with a cross-job consistency statistic; and (E) compilation/execution integrity. Each gates on significance, so honest operation raises no alarm. We evaluate in faithful simulation and on three production IBM Heron processors, and bound the physical attack surface with a systematic negative map: most physical-layer attacks return statistically null, the exception an implemented, measured within-job feed-forward covert-channel primitive. Every detector is also evaluated against an adaptive attacker with full knowledge of it. To our knowledge this is the first unified statistical-and-behavioral detection layer for the QEC layer and classical control stack of a quantum computing system, demonstrated on production hardware.

title: The most entangled states of four and seven qubits
summary:
Pure states of four and seven qubits cannot be maximally entangled across every balanced bipartition; we determine how entangled they can be on average. For four qubits we prove the conjecture of Higuchi and Sudbery: the mean von Neumann entropy of the three $2|2$ cuts is at most $1+\tfrac12\log_2 3$ bits, with equality exactly on the local-unitary orbits of their state $M_4$ and its complex conjugate. For seven qubits the mean purity of the 35 balanced $3|4$ cuts is at least $121/917$ and their mean entropy is at most $2.965356029\ldots$ bits, each with a unique optimiser up to local unitaries and qubit permutations. The two optimisers are distinct members of one icosahedral family, so minimum purity and maximum entropy select different states.
  The proofs bound moments of the marginal spectra by positive identities on several copies of the state, some of them spin flipped, and bound the entropy by a polynomial in those moments. The four-qubit maximum has an analytic proof; the seven-qubit proofs, and some of the four-qubit refinements below, are computer-assisted, with exact arithmetic and rigorous error bounds. We also prove the Gour--Wallach conjecture for Rényi entropies of all orders, with the maximiser changing from $M_4$ to cluster states at $q_*\approx1.588$, and obtain sharp Tsallis bounds, mixed-state bounds and quantitative stability.

title: Structural Lower Bounds for Quantum Property Estimation with Persistent Memory
summary:
In quantum property estimation, an experimenter estimates $\operatorname{Tr}(Oρ)$ for a family of observables from independent copies of an unknown state $ρ$ simultaneously to additive error $ε$. While quantum memory can dramatically reduce sample complexity, understanding the power of a modest register that remains coherent throughout an adaptive experiment has remained an open challenge because existing frameworks require optimizing over the infinite space of measurement trees.
  We overcome this barrier by developing a backward-induction framework based on operator resolvents. Rather than tracking path-dependent memory states across rounds, resolvent regularization cancels internal memory trajectories exactly, reducing the lower bound to an algebraic certificate computed directly from the target observables with sharp $Ω(1/ε^2)$ scaling.
  Our structural rule charges only the retained dimension $K$ under arbitrary adaptive instruments and unrestricted memory lifetime. Via symmetry reductions, it yields polynomial-size linear programs that establish the optimal linear $Ω(D/(Kε^2))$ trade-off for the $D^2-1$ Paulis, eliminating the cubic loss in prior bounds. For growing weight-$w$ Pauli strings ($w=\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$) and quadratic Majorana cross-correlations, it proves lower bounds of $Ω(3^w/ε^2)$ and $Ω(n^2/(ε^2(1+\ln n)^2))$ against an indefinitely persistent memory of dimension $K=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$. These bounds match memoryless or commuting estimators within polylogarithmic factors, demonstrating that rank constraints on the persistent register fundamentally throttle observable overlap and prevent a modest coherent memory from overcoming the sample complexity barrier.

title: Classical records and Bell correlations in a dynamically formed quantum body
summary: Competing quantum contacts can create a boundary that was absent from the specification of a subsystem. We construct approximately isolated bodies from bare field vacuum and zero-centred contact packets. A binding contribution with vanishing mean energy density nevertheless changes a bounded formation signal by order one at the same clock. On the formed material spins and their original memories, coarse collective records precede an all-outcome Bell violation. The field evolves dynamically, with the finite bath, residual boundary interaction, failed records and preparation costs retained. The result connects dynamical subsystem formation, classical collective records and microscopic nonlocality, with polynomial resources in the stated preparation and measurement class.

title: Symmetry-guided algorithms for variational quantum optimization
summary: Quantum numbers associated with symmetries classify quantum states and identify the sectors relevant to a given simulation. Generic hardware-efficient ansatzes do not necessarily preserve the quantum numbers and may therefore explore states outside the target sector. We develop symmetry-guided algorithms based on the quantum-accessible Hilbert--Schmidt asymmetry (\(\AHS\)), which quantifies the deviation of a quantum state from invariance under a specified symmetry group. This quantity guides the optimization toward a highly reduced symmetry-based target sector, without enforcing the symmetry on the preparation circuit. We demonstrate the approach as a proof of principle in variational quantum eigensolver calculations targeting singlet ground states with collective SU(2) symmetry. The applications include a five-qubit \(S\)-wave \(p+{}^3\mathrm{He}\) two-cluster Hamiltonian, deduced from \textit{ab initio} many-body calculations, and collective spin models with up to 12 particles, which provide a many-particle benchmark of asymmetry-guided optimization. Across these applications, \(\AHS\)-based guidance increases the singlet probability. Overall, the proposed algorithms improve energy accuracy during optimization and ground-state fidelity compared with direct energy minimization, with substantial fidelity improvements in the larger spin systems. These results demonstrate the utility of an asymmetry objective determined by the group action, independently of the Hamiltonian energy, for improving the reliability of variational quantum optimization.

authors: Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente
title: Efficiently tracking errors and outcomes in universal quantum circuits
summary: We present a method for efficient simulation of error propagation and decoding in universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits under stochastic Pauli noise, requiring only that the circuit has a high fault distance and that all logical non-Clifford operations are implemented by physical T, CS and CCZ gates. This is achieved using modified Pauli frame-based error tracking in which the frame contains no logical information. Decoding success is identified by verifying that the Pauli frame is still logically trivial after decoding. Using the results of Ref. [1] and the observation that the distribution of non-logical measurement outcomes in the circuit is independent of the logical state, we show that we can accurately sample all detector outcomes. Our approach can also simulate circuits containing adaptive operations conditioned on logical measurements, provided these measurements have a known outcome distribution. This applies to the majority of adaptive operations such as state teleportation and preparation by measurement. Our method only detects decoding failures and so is consistent with complexity-theoretic expectations as it cannot be used to sample from the noiseless outcome distribution of the logical circuit.

title: Quantum Advantage in Sensing and Imaging through Coherent Nuisance Suppression
summary: Many sensing and imaging problems must contend with unknown nuisance parameters such as aberrations, background fields, and drift, and the cost of removing these noise sources can dominate the sample budget. In contrast to classical receivers, a quantum receiver can processes samples jointly to directly access observables in which common nuisance is suppressed. We introduce a relational Fourier sampling algorithm for optimal, source-independent imaging with a programmable quantum camera, which uses quantum pixels and a quantum computer to capture and process photon states. We demonstrate its relevance for general astronomical imaging as well as super-resolution and transient-object tracking through drifting atmospheric turbulence. A quantum camera that resolves an optical wavefront across $2^q$ spatial modes using $q$ receiving qubits, with a full-rank and strongly-correlated nuisance over those modes, can yield an exponential sample-complexity reduction of $\exp[Ω(2^q)]$. For typical seeing conditions at leading ground-based observatories, we predict more than three orders of magnitude fewer photons to resolve point-source positions using only 15 processing qubits and a depth-9 circuit. Our work identifies coherent nuisance suppression as a novel mechanism for provable quantum advantage with direct relevance to many sensing tasks.

title: Hardware Demonstration of Neural-Surrogated Quantum-Enhanced MCMC for Large-Scale Constrained Boltzmann Sampling
summary: Neural-surrogated quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo (QeMCMC) uses neural networks trained on samples from the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to accelerate Boltzmann sampling. A divide-and-conquer strategy extends this approach to larger systems, but independently optimizing QAOA parameters for each subproblem is costly. In this paper, we develop a hardware-efficient implementation of neural-surrogated QeMCMC and demonstrate it using an IBM Quantum Heron r2 processor. Experiments with $N=144$ binary variables reveal faster autocorrelation decay for appropriate subproblem sizes while exposing challenges in neural-surrogate learning for larger blocks. We then extend the demonstration to a system with $N=1064$, where the autocorrelation decay rate per MCMC step is approximately $5.2$ and $12.3$ times those of global and local Kawasaki dynamics, respectively. These results demonstrate faster autocorrelation decay in a system exceeding one thousand variables using samples generated on quantum hardware.

title: Algorithmic Wave-Particle Duality: Pathfinding in Welded Trees is Hard
comment: Subsumes our prior works https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26712 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20651
summary:
In the welded trees problem, an algorithm navigates a randomly labeled graph formed from two binary trees joined at their leaves through a "weld" of connecting edges. A quantum walk can navigate from root to root exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, recording its path destroys the constructive interference responsible for the speedup, leaving open whether some quantum algorithm can efficiently find a path between the roots.
  We prove that, for trees of height $n$, the quantum query complexity of finding a path between the roots with constant probability is $\tildeΘ(2^{n/3})$. This establishes an algorithmic wave-particle duality, adapting the double-slit experiment to the high-complexity regime: interference between many paths lets a quantum algorithm reach the exit efficiently, but finding a single path (the algorithmic analog of the route of a particle) requires exponentially many queries. Furthermore, the bound is tight, matching the cost of a quantum algorithm that finds collisions between paths from each root to the weld. Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle to track the information about the graph that an algorithm retains and forgets. We show that the compressed database remains close to a space of states that do not record a path between the roots by bounding the error introduced by each compressed oracle query.

title: Rotated-Frame Determinant Discovery for Ground- and Excited-State Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction
comment: Main text and Supporting Information, 47 pages, 6 figures
summary: Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction (QSCI) constructs a variational determinant space from measurements of a prepared electronic state, but finite-shot sampling can repeatedly observe high-probability determinants, limiting efficient discovery of configurations important for an accurate selected-CI description. We introduce rotate--sample--unrotate (RSU) determinant discovery, in which the same state is sampled in complementary orbital frames and the observed rotated determinants generate a finite set of candidates in the canonical basis. The Hamiltonian is then diagonalized in an orthonormal selected-CI space without enumerating the full determinant space. State-targeted orbital frames are constructed from an initial selected-CI wavefunction and its external residual. For excited states, we combine RSU with the generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) to prepare target-specific sampling states. Candidate GQE circuits are evaluated by classical selected-CI diagonalization in finite sampled spaces, so the quantum procedure requires only state preparation and determinant sampling. For N$_2$, exact-state controls isolate the determinant-discovery effect: at the stretched geometry, residual-natural-orbital RSU reaches chemical accuracy with 5,000 shots, compared with 20,000 shots for conventional QSCI. The improvement persists with approximate GQE-prepared states and is also observed for target excited states. These results demonstrate improved finite-shot determinant discovery in QSCI for both ground and excited states.

title: Norm Bounds on Sums of Positive Operators with Applications to Monogamy Games and Quantum Key Distribution
summary: Bounding the acceptance probabilities of quantum measurements is a recurring task in quantum information theory. An acceptance probability averaged over a random measurement setting can be bounded uniformly over the input state by the operator norm of an average of positive semidefinite operators. We prove a general inequality for such norms, valid for arbitrary finite families of positive semidefinite operators and averaging distributions. We give two applications of our operator-norm inequality. First, we determine the sharp robustness threshold for the parallel BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement game. For error thresholds $β,γ\in[0,1/2]$, when the two players may make at most $βn$ and $γn$ errors, respectively, the optimal winning probability decays exponentially if $(1-2β)^2+(1-2γ)^2>1$, tends to one exponentially fast under the reverse strict inequality, and remains bounded away from zero on the boundary. Second, we establish the achievability of every asymptotic key rate $0<R<1- 2h_2(γ)$ for one-sided device-independent BB84 quantum key distribution with tolerated bit-error rate $γ$ and asymptotically optimal reconciliation, where $h_2(\cdot)$ is the binary entropy function. Alice's measurements are trusted, while Bob may perform an arbitrary joint measurement depending on the entire basis string, subject to the protocol's receipt and isolation requirements. This recovers the usual BB84 rate in this model.

title: The Structure of Shared Classical Facts in Quantum Systems
summary: Perfectly matching local outcomes need not constitute a nondisturbing shared classical record. For finite-dimensional multipartite states, we prove that nontrivial exact records are equivalent to a spectrum sharing structure with a unique finest decomposition into locally distinguishable sectors, where entanglement may persist. For a fixed complete pointer, exact sharing is equivalent to strong quantum Darwinism together with global nondisturbance, while spectrum broadcast structure additionally requires conditional independence. Arbitrarily weak full-rank admixtures eliminate exact sharing, but two-sided distance bounds quantify robustness through disturbance and disagreement, while information bounds connect accurate local readouts to observer consensus.

title: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization via Density Matrix Renormalization Group
summary: We introduce SqDMRG, which combines sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). SqDMRG expands the sampled determinant space into a product of fragment spaces constructed from the samples, and solves the Hamiltonian in this product space using DMRG. We demonstrate the method on benzene pentamer and decamer clusters using classical reference samples, and on the pentamer using quantum samples obtained from the IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processor ibm phoenix. It achieves sub-kcal/mol accuracy with far fewer configurations than direct diagonalization.

title: Collectively pumped superradiant laser with coherence scaling beyond the standard quantum limit
comment: 36 pages, 16 figures. Submitted to Physical Review X
summary: For more than half a century, the standard quantum limit (SQL) was thought to limit the laser coherence $\mathfrak{C}$ -- the number of photons emitted from the laser into the beam in one coherence time -- to a scaling $Θ(μ^2)$, where $μ$ is the mean number of optical-frequency excitations stored inside the laser. However, recently it has been shown [Baker et al., Nat. Phys. 17, 179 (2021)] that the Heisenberg limit -- an achievable ultimate limit set by quantum mechanics for the task of producing a beam with the standard properties of a laser beam -- is $\mathfrak{C}=Θ(μ^4)$, a quadratic enhancement. So far, proposals to demonstrate beyond-SQL scaling of $\mathfrak{C}$ have been limited to circuit QED, at microwave frequencies (i.e., a maser). Here, we introduce a class of generalized far-above-threshold (FAT) laser models, obtained by replacing the ordinary bosonic lowering operator $\hat{a}$ by a general lowering operator $\hat{L}$ in the superoperators appearing in the master equation that governs the FAT laser dynamics. We then show that an optical-frequency superradiant laser in the bad-cavity limit, with feedback-controlled collective pumping, realizes one such model, in which $\hat{L}$ is identified with the collective superradiant lowering operator $\hat{J}$. This model can surpass the SQL scaling, with the coherence exhibiting a scaling as large as $\mathfrak{C}= Θ(μ^{8/3})$ in the optimal parameter regime. Here, in the bad-cavity limit, $μ\approx N/2$, where $N$ is the number of superradiant atoms.

title: Quantum Key Exchange from Public Quantum Money
summary: Two-message quantum key exchange (2QKE) cannot be realized in a statistically secure way, and therefore some computational assumptions are required. So far, the known weakest assumption for 2QKE is the existence of one-way functions (OWFs). Can we construct 2QKE from a weaker assumption than OWFs? In this paper, we give the first complete characterization of 2QKE. We show that the following four primitives are (existentially) equivalent: everlasting-secure 2QKE, standard 2QKE, efficiently-verifiable state puzzles (EV-StatePuzzs), and one-time secure digital signatures with quantum signatures and signing keys. Because EV-StatePuzzs are potentially weaker than OWFs [Kretschmer, Qian and Tal 2025], the equivalence implies that 2QKE are potentially weaker than OWFs. Moreover, our result shows the equivalence between standard 2QKE and everlasting-secure 2QKE, which means that everlasting security comes for free. Finally, one-shot signatures, quantum lightning, and public-key quantum money mini-schemes imply EV-StatePuzzs, and therefore, our result also gives a new lowerbound, namely everlasting-secure 2QKE, of these public-key unclonable primitives. We also show that one-shot signatures imply QPKE with quantum public keys. [Kitagawa, Morimae,Nishimaki and Yamakawa, 2024] constructed QPKE with quantum public keys from OWFs, and it was open whether QPKE with quantum public keys can be constructed from an assumption weaker than or incomparable to OWFs. Our result gives a potential answer to this question since one-shot signatures seem to be incomparable with OWFs. Moreover, QPKE constructed from one-shot signatures has an additional functionality, which we call certified freeze, that allows the receiver to publish a publicly verifiable classical certificate that computationally binds the receiver to an upper bound on the total number of distinct valid ciphertexts under its verification key.

title: Shadow bootstrapping: Nearly minimal-setting pure-state tomography with shallow Clifford measurements
summary: We present a pure-state tomography algorithm that uses a nearly minimal number of measurement settings while achieving optimal sample complexity with nonadaptive single-copy shallow Clifford measurements. For an arbitrary $n$-qubit pure state $|ψ\rangle \in \mathbb{C}^{d}$, where $d=2^n$, the algorithm uses $O(d/ε)$ copies and $\widetilde{O}(1)$ measurement settings to output a state vector $|\hatψ\rangle$ satisfying $1-|\langleψ|\hatψ\rangle|^2\leε$ with high probability. Each measurement is implemented by a Clifford circuit of depth $O(\log n)$. Reusing each measurement setting allows the data to be stored compactly as per-basis outcome histograms. Given these histograms, classical post-processing runs in $\widetilde{O}(d)$ time. Our key technique, \textit{shadow bootstrapping}, uses the current estimate to reduce the variance of subsequent residual estimation, enabling progressively more accurate reconstruction with only a constant number of new measurement settings per stage.

title: Classical Clifford+T Sampling without Computing Marginals
summary: We introduce a new exact classical sampling algorithm for Clifford+T circuits, called T-by-T sampling. For a circuit with T-count t, it reduces sampling to evaluating 2t amplitudes of circuits with successively increasing T-counts 1,2,...,t, without the need to compute costly marginal probabilities. Crucially, the number of amplitude evaluations is completely independent of the surrounding Clifford structure. This makes T-by-T sampling well suited for use together with low-rank stabiliser decompositions, which enable efficient amplitude evaluations as long as the T-count is not too high. In that sense, T-by-T sampling is an improvement over the gate-by-gate sampling technique introduced by Bravyi, Gosset, and Liu (Phys. Rev. Lett. 128, 2022), where the number of amplitudes instead scales with the number of non-monomial operations such as Hadamard gates, which can remain large even in circuits with low stabiliser rank. Concretely, T-by-T sampling offers significant speedups in regimes where T gates are embedded within large Clifford computations. This makes it well suited for applications such as simulating quantum error correction experiments, which typically have lower T complexity but involve extensive Clifford operations and measurements. In particular, we show how T-by-T sampling allows us to take samples from recent end-to-end magic state cultivation circuits with escape up to distance 19 in a couple of seconds.

title: A Post-Quantum Interactive Hashing Theorem
summary: Interactive hashing, introduced by Ostrovsky, Venkatesan, and Yung [OVY93], is a building block in many cryptographic protocols, including perfectly hiding commitments from one-way permutations [NOVY92]. Its multi-output generalization is a key ingredient in constructions of statistical zero-knowledge arguments for NP and statistically hiding commitments from arbitrary one-way functions [NOV06,HR07]. In this note, we give a post-quantum security proof for this multi-output interactive hashing protocol with arbitrary relations.

title: Robust Geometric Gates for QCCD Architecture
summary: The trapped-ion quantum charge-coupled device (QCCD) is a promising route toward scalable quantum computing. However, the frequency offset during shuttling operations introduce significant decoherence and control errors, severely degrading gate fidelity on transported ions. Here, using a room-temperature planar chip trap, we demonstrate a robust and universal single-qubit gate set in the QCCD architecture. Based on a recently proposed path-optimizable noncyclic geometric scheme, we show that dynamic noise is strongly suppressed even when multiple shuttling operations are interleaved with gate execution, achieving substantially higher fidelities than conventional dynamical gates. This robustness is further validated in a multi-ion system containing up to 33 qubits. With inherent robustness and adaptability to varying shuttle distances and ion numbers, our work offers a plug-and-play solution for building robust quantum primitives for the QCCD platform.

title: Spatial Cost of Recovering a Fusion Qubit in a Critical Spin Chain
summary: Vanishing-error recovery of a fusion qubit from a fixed-sector ground doublet of four Kramers--Wannier defects in a critical Ising chain requires at least the shorter three-defect span of physical spins to leading order. Across arbitrary preselected spin sets and unrestricted joint decoding, this bound holds when the thermodynamic limit precedes large spacings at fixed positive ratios. An exact interval decoder attains it. Collective records of both logical axes in the complement force successful near-minimal supports to concentrate in density on a leading-order shortest interval.

title: Resetting a Superconducting Qubit with a Compact Colder Resistive Dissipator below the Qubit Frequency
summary: Efficient qubit reset has become a key requirement for large-scale superconducting quantum processors, as initialization fidelity increasingly lags behind gate performance and quantum error correction demands rapid, high-fidelity state re-initialization. This work proposes a compact on-chip dissipator consisting of two transmon dissipation modes and a thin-film resistor, and experimentally demonstrates an unconditional reset protocol. With no additional control lines and negligible impact on the qubit $T_1$, the effective temperature of the transmon qubit is reduced from $49$~mK to $35$~mK. Quantum process tomography is employed to benchmark the reset process, achieving a process error of $0.0028$. This reset protocol is robust to pulse parameter deviations, thereby relaxing calibration requirements. The dissipator architecture provides a practical, calibration-friendly reset solution for large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

title: Connection of surface code patches based on entanglement distillation without postselection
summary: Distributed quantum computing is a promising approach for overcoming the scalability limitations of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Entanglement distillation, a process that extracts higher-fidelity entangled states from noisy ones, plays a key role in distributed quantum computing. However, simple distillation protocols typically rely on postselection, which poses practical challenges for implementation. Here, we propose a scheme for distributed surface-code quantum computing that benefits from entanglement distillation even without postselection. Numerical simulations show that the logical error rates in the proposed scheme are lower than those in the setting without distillation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the logical error rates can be suppressed further by exploiting the asymmetry between spacelike and timelike errors in the surface code. The proposed scheme offers a practical and simple approach to distributed quantum computing with surface codes.

title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression
summary: Quantum errors in noisy environments remain a major obstacle to advancing quantum information technology. Standard quantum error correction requires massive ancillary qubit overhead, motivating the need for hardware-efficient mitigation strategies. In this work, we propose a framework for dynamical quantum error correction at the circuit level, requiring no logical encoding or ancillary qubits. By extending a geometric framework (originally developed for creating dynamical error-correcting gates at the control pulse level) to the discrete dynamics of digital circuits, we map the accumulation of coherent errors to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. We demonstrate that inserting deterministically optimized twirling gate sequences actively shapes these trajectories, utilizing destructive interference to keep the accumulated error bounded with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(1)$. This deterministic path-shaping suppresses circuit errors fundamentally differently than the stochastic random-walk behavior of standard randomized compiling with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Furthermore, we show that this circuit-level dynamical correction synergizes with pulse-level robust control, providing an analytical bridge between continuous noise dynamics and discrete quantum compilation. This research illuminates pathways to achieving highly noise-resistant quantum circuits prior to the era of fault tolerance.

title: Spatial Path Superposition: A No-Cloning Perspective on MIMO-Inspired Spatial Diversity
comment: Accepted manuscript for publication in Frontiers in Communications and Networks. This work has been funded by the European Union under Horizon Europe ERC-CoG grant QNattyNet ("Quantum-Native Communication Networks: from Quantum Message to Quantum Functioning"), n. 101169850. Details at https://qnattynet.quantuminternet.it
summary: Spatial diversity is a key mechanism in classical Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) communications, where multiple propagation alternatives provide redundant observations that improve reliability in noisy environments. A direct translation of this principle to quantum communications is forbidden by the no-cloning theorem, since an unknown quantum state cannot be copied and transmitted through independent links. In this Perspective article, we argue that spatial path superposition provides a no-cloning-compatible analogue of the spatial-diversity principle of MIMO. Rather than duplicating the transmitted quantum state, a quantum carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple communication links, so that alternative spatial evolutions are experienced in quantum superposition. In this framework, classical redundancy is replaced by spatial coherence, and the communication link itself becomes part of the quantum dynamics. Indeed, spatial coherence can enhance the fidelity of the received quantum state, providing the quantum counterpart of the classical diversity gain, and can be converted into bipartite and multipartite entanglement during propagation. This implies that, under suitable coherent path control, noisy channel evolutions can contribute constructively to entanglement generation. This Perspective identifies spatial path superposition as a quantum-native primitive for the Quantum Internet, linking no-cloning-compatible spatial diversity, fidelity enhancement, entanglement generation, and coherent path control.

title: Semi-Device-Independent Certification of multi-qubit Entangled Basis Measurement
summary: The entangled basis measurement plays a pivotal role in fundamental information-processing tasks, such as dense coding, quantum teleportation, and entanglement swapping. Consequently, certifying such measurements in a device-independent manner remains an important task. In this work, we present a semi-device-independent (SDI) protocol in a prepare-and-measure (PM) scenario for certifying a class of m-qubit entangled basis measurements. Specifically, we consider a tripartite PM scenario featuring two senders and one receiver, where each sender sends an arbitrary number of 2^m inputs and the receiver performs a measurement with 2^m outcomes. We adopt a classical causal model framework to demonstrate the non-classicality of quantum measurements. We introduce nonlinear witnesses in classical causal models and demonstrate that the optimal quantum value exceeds the classical bounds. Further, we demonstrate that the optimal quantum value of the witness SDI certify the entangled basis measurement and the prepared states of the two senders.

title: Improved Exact and Approximate Quantum Fourier Transforms from Multiplication
summary:
In the world of quantum computing, quantum Fourier transform (QFT) has been one of the most important subroutines for quantum algorithms, as exemplified by Shor's factoring algorithms and phase estimation (which in itself has been used as a primitive in various quantum algorithms). In fact most of the well known quantum algorithms can be divided into two classes, QFT based algorithms and search based algorithms.
  The usual circuit for QFT (covered in almost every basic quantum algorithms course) needs $O(q^2)$ gates (and $O(q)$ qubits) to perform the exact Fourier transform over $\mathbb{F}_{2^q}$. Cleve and Watrous (FOCS 2000) improved this gate count to $O(q (\log q)^2 (\log \log q))$ using the integer multiplication algorithm in $O(n (\log n) (\log \log n))$ time for two $n$-bit integers (best known at that time). Our first main result shows that this gate count can be improved to $O(q (\log q))$. In fact, if there is a multiplication circuit, to multiply two $n$-bit integers, with $O(n (\log n)^α)$ gates; we get a QFT circuit with $O(q (\log q)^α)$ gates (improving upon $O(q (\log q)^{α+ 1})$) gates from the construction of Cleve and Watrous). Given the recent claim by OpenAI about integer multiplication, this opens up the possibility of having a QFT circuit with $o \left( q (\log q)\right)$ gates.
  On approximating the QFT over $\ZZ/(2^q \ZZ)$, the result of Ahokas, Cleve and Hales (ERATO 2003) showed that an approximating circuit can be built with $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^{α+1} \right)$ gates, where $ε$ is the approximating parameter. Our second main result again improves this to $O \left( q (\log \log(q/\varepsilon))^α \right)$ gates.

title: Helium States in a CAS(2,2) Subspace Inspired by Quantum Photonics
summary: We present a four-mode Fock-state photonics implementation of the variational quantum deflation (VQD) algorithm to calculate the ground-state and excited-state energies for the neutral helium atom in a CAS(2,2) Subspace. Its CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space is encoded into a bosonic Fock-space representation and subsequently optimized using a continuous-variable quantum circuit. The circuit architecture under study is constructed of single-mode phase shifts, beam splitters, and cross-Kerr interactions. The variational circuit is initialized in the Fock state $\ket{1100}$ and its performance is benchmarked against exact diagonalization of the active-space configuration-interaction (CASCI) Hamiltonian. We also extend the method to optimize from the first to three excited states of the helium atom with the aid of the variational quantum deflation $(VQD)$ method in a CAS(2,2). We then investigate the performance of this circuit architecture as a basis for implementing the VQD method. In the ideal noiseless simulation setting, we see that the survival probability of the ground and the excited states within the target $CAS$ subspace is unity, because the total photon number and the photon number in the two spin sectors $α$ and $β$ are preserved. We demonstrate that the proposed approach enables the determination of the ground and excited-state energies within the CAS(2,2) electronic Hilbert space using a continuous-variable quantum circuit and the variational quantum deflation ($VQD$) algorithm, while satisfying the orthogonality conditions with negligible errors.

title: Beyond the Gap: What Imaginary-Time Evolution Reveals About the Edge of the Continuum
summary: The spectral gap, the energy separating the ground state from the first excitation, governs many quantum phenomena, yet it is far harder to compute than the ground state. We propose a mathematically rigorous method for extracting the gap from imaginary-time evolution in infinite-dimensional Hamiltonians, where the first excitation typically marks the edge of a continuous spectrum. We show that a gap is not automatically detected: detection depends on how the initial state and observable couple the ground state to excitations at the bottom of the continuum. When this coupling follows a power law, the gap is recovered together with a logarithmic correction whose coefficient yields the exponent of the spectral density near the edge of the continuum, which reflects the physics of the excitations. We confirm both predictions numerically for an exactly solvable model. Our results offer a new numerical approach to many-body quantum physics, in which both the gap and the threshold exponent are obtained merely at the cost of a ground-state calculation.

title: Universally Certifying Partially Self-Correcting Quantum Memories in 3D Translation-Invariant Stabilizer Codes
summary: Achieving passive protection of quantum information at finite temperature is a central problem at the intersection of quantum information and quantum many-body physics. Yet a general, computable criterion for determining self-correcting behavior directly from the form of local interactions remains elusive. Here we develop a unified algebraic-geometric framework for certifying partial self-correction in three-dimensional translation-invariant local stabilizer codes, encompassing the cubic code as a special case. From the algebraic curves defined by the codes' defining polynomials, we construct valuation matrices on the boundaries of their normalized projective closures and derive a computable rank criterion. Together with a polynomial-time decoder, this criterion guarantees super-Arrhenius memory lifetimes for code families satisfying it under the specified local Davies dynamics. We apply the framework to certify several classes of partially self-correcting quantum memories, including nearest-neighbor models with stabilizer weight as low as six and long memory lifetimes at modest system sizes. These results establish an algebraic-geometric connection between local stabilizer structure and the recoverability of quantum information at finite temperature, providing a systematic approach to certifying and designing passive quantum memories.

title: Quantum Advantage needs Multiple Perspectives
summary: The origin of the quantum speedup is a topic of ongoing research. We propose a logical criterion for the possibility of a speedup within the continuous-variable and odd-prime qudit settings. There, Wigner function nonnegativity signals the possibility of efficient classical simulation in the state-injection scenario. We consider representations of quadrature/Weyl measurements in a single von Neumann algebra that reproduce the Born statistics in a particular state. If in that state, the set-theoretic universe of the algebra is ZFC-satisfiable, i.e. every ZFC-theorem holds with unit probability, all measurement contexts can be represented in a single commutative algebra of `beables'. Furthermore, the statistics admit a noncontextual hidden variable model, ensuring Wigner nonnegativity for two or more modes or qudits. For a single mode, a stronger notion of linear representation ensures commutativity, and with it, ZFC-satisfiability independently of the state, as well as Wigner nonnegativity. In consequence, in any setting that cannot be efficiently simulated, it must be impossible to merge the models associated with every context into a single ZFC-satisfiable one: quantum advantage needs multiple perspectives.

title: A Variational Quantum Algorithm for Multi-Skill Project Scheduling
summary: Job scheduling is an NP-hard optimization problem with clear industrial relevance. In practice, distributing work across a team is not only about meeting deadlines or improving productivity; it also affects fatigue, stress, and employee well-being. Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) provide a promising way to address these problems through QUBO formulations, although their scalability on near-term NISQ hardware is still limited by Hilbert-space growth and barren plateaus. In this work, we simulate a VQA for a realistic Multi-Skill Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (MS-RCPSP), including worker capacities, skill matrices, task priorities, deadlines, and calendar stability during rescheduling. To keep the problem within a near-term circuit size, we use a temporal batch decomposition that solves one day at a time, propagates the remaining workload, and combines it with a logarithmic binary encoding that keeps every batch at or below 30 qubits. Because the ground state of a QUBO Hamiltonian is a computational basis state, entanglement is not required to represent the solution, raising the question of whether it helps or hinders ansatz training. We address this question by comparing the linear and brick-wall entangling topologies of a hardware-efficient ansatz with an entanglement-free reference that has the same number of parameters and by training every configuration with COBYLA and with Adam using SPSA gradient estimation. For the instance and initialization studied, the entanglement-free reference produced feasible schedules under both optimizers. With COBYLA, it produced the feasible schedule closest to the required workload at a fraction of the simulation cost of the entangled topologies, indicating that entanglement did not improve the solutions found by the VQA.

title: Parrondo's paradox for three discrete-time quantum walks with distinct shift operators
comment: submitted to Quantum Information Processing on July 27, 2026
summary: Parrondo's paradox describes a surprising phenomenon in which certain combinations of biased quantum walks result in an unexpected reversal of their bias direction. To date, research on this effect has predominantly focused on one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walks that employ fixed sequences of two or three quantum coins, paired with a single shift operator. In this work, we first introduce a wide class of unitary shift operators which allow for three movement options (left, right or stay in place) of a walker in one time step, and we then demonstrate that Parrondo's paradox can also arise with a single coin and three distinct shift operators. Furthermore, we investigate how this paradox influences the time evolution of quantum entanglement between the walker and the coin in such quantum walks.

title: Equivalence of Correlated Catalytic and Marginal Asymptotic Transformations in Quantum Resource Theories
summary: We prove that correlated-catalytic state conversion is possible if and only if the marginal asymptotic conversion rate is at least one. Under general operational assumptions, this equivalence holds for arbitrary states in broad classes of entanglement, coherence, and magic theories. It reduces the characterization of correlated-catalytic convertibility to the computation of marginal asymptotic rates, and yields transitivity and equality of catalytic and marginal conversion rates. Under local operations and classical communication, we fully characterize correlated-catalytic conversion from arbitrary bipartite states to entangled pure states in terms of distillable entanglement. We show that correlated catalysts cannot increase the distillable entanglement or distillable secret key of any bipartite state, and in particular cannot make bound entanglement distillable. Extending our construction to adaptive communication protocols, we further prove that correlated catalysts cannot enhance the two-way private-state generation capacity of any finite-dimensional quantum channel.

title: Compatibility of Pauli Observables
summary: Given an arbitrary finite family of Pauli observables, how sharply can they be approximated by a single measurement? We derive an exact state-space correspondence that characterises the resulting sharpness tradeoffs, establishing a link between incompatibility and preparation uncertainty. In particular, suitable ensembles of quantum states determine the full compatibility region and generate explicit parent measurements through Pauli conjugation and classical randomisation. The compatibility region depends only on the anti-commutativity graph and determines all nonuniform tradeoffs under standard noise models, including depolarising, probabilistic and generalised noise. We show that optimal sharpness tradeoffs are determined by spectral problems for signed Pauli Hamiltonians, whose ground states supply the seeds for optimal parent measurements. The correspondence also shows that magic is necessary to attain the full compatibility region of every noncommuting Pauli family. We quantify the resulting sharpness advantage and relate it to the reduced robustness of magic. Finally, we apply the framework to several structured Pauli families, obtaining exact compatibility characterisations and explicit optimal parents.

title: Discovering correlated error mechanisms: data-driven augmentation of detector error models improving decoding
summary: Accurate decoder priors are essential for high-performance quantum error correction. Theoretical noise models inevitably omit physically relevant error mechanisms, most notably correlated errors, which appear consistently in experimental error budgets yet are absent from standard models. We introduce a data-driven method for augmenting detector error models (DEMs) by discovering entirely new error mechanisms directly from experimental detector-firing statistics, going beyond most existing approaches that merely refine the probabilities of already-known mechanisms. Our method generates candidates by combining pairs of existing mechanisms as building blocks, then filters and validates them using pairwise and higher-order detector correlations. Crucially, this construction provides each newly discovered mechanism with a well-defined logical effect derived from the constituent error mechanisms, enabling its direct use in decoding. Furthermore, each mechanism is accompanied by a natural decomposition into lower-order components, preserving compatibility with the original decoder. This is particularly valuable in settings that rely on correlated graph-based decoders such as correlated matching. We evaluate the method on surface-code simulations with correlated noise and correlated-matching decoding, demonstrating that, in a realistic near-term noise scenario, DEM augmentation increases the Lambda parameter by 20% across code distances 7-15 and reduces the logical error rate by 75% at code distance 15 relative to the unaugmented DEM. On experimental data from Google's superconducting device, the augmented DEM increases the Lambda parameter by 9% across code distances 5-7 and yields a reduction of 14% in logical error rate over the baseline for distance 7. To our knowledge, this is the first data-driven DEM augmentation method that produces decomposed hyperedges with assigned logical effects.

title: Noise-regularized training of quantum circuit Born machines under a finite shot budget
summary: Quantum circuit Born machines (QCBMs) can learn distributions that are hard to sample from classically, but their value depends on generalizing from finite training data. Here, we study how hardware noise affects this generalization. We show that, for any noise process, the generalization gap of a QCBM trained with the maximum mean discrepancy is bounded by the complexity of the distributions the noisy model can reach. Scrambled local Pauli noise contracts this complexity but biases the model towards the uniform distribution, so residual noise acts as a regularizer whose optimal strength can be intermediate. We propose GENIE, a framework that realizes a chosen noise level with capped error mitigation and selects it during training from held-out data within a fixed execution budget, with provably bounded regret. In simulations on synthetic and census data, GENIE stays close to the best of four noise-control strategies, whereas every fixed noise level falls short in many settings.

title: Precision Limits and Non-Gaussian Advantage in Optical Phase Estimation under Preparation Constraints
summary: In optical quantum metrology, the scaling of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) with the mean photon number is a standard benchmark for relating precision to probe resources. For phase estimation, Heisenberg scaling corresponds to a quadratic growth of the QFI with the mean photon number, which Gaussian probes can approach. Interestingly, certain non-Gaussian probes can exhibit arbitrarily large QFI even at fixed mean photon number. Here, we clarify the resource requirements underlying this behavior by introducing a constraint that separates physically admissible states from inadmissible ones: an envelope on the photon-number distribution that arises naturally from the physical limitations of state-generation methods. Building on this constraint and considering pure single-mode probes, we define a resource quantity, $N_\mathrm{RMS}$, fixed by the preparation constraints, and derive a finite bound on the QFI whose Heisenberg scaling is attainable. We identify a genuine metrological advantage of non-Gaussian states over Gaussian probes subject to the same constraints. Finally, we illustrate these results with an optical preparation model based on a universal gate set.

title: Efficient quantum ultraspherical transform and a well-conditioned quantum spectral method
summary: Solving differential equations is a promising application of quantum computing. Spectral methods, where the solution is represented by coefficients in a basis, are particularly well suited to quantum solvers because their structured discretizations can enable efficient linear-algebra operations while providing rapid convergence. Their quantum implementation, however, requires an efficient transform between amplitudes encoding function values and amplitudes encoding expansion coefficients. This work develops two key components of a quantum spectral method. First, we construct the quantum ultraspherical transform (QUT) for orthonormal ultraspherical polynomials, a basis that supports sparse and well-conditioned discretizations of differential equations. For the basis parameters $m=0$ and $1$, this transform reduces to the discrete cosine and sine transforms with known efficient circuits. Our contribution covers every fixed integer $m\geq2$: for dimensions $N$ with $N+m=2^n$, where $n$ is the number of qubits, the QUT achieves error at most $\varepsilon$ using a gate count polynomial in $n$ and $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. The construction builds on the quantum Fourier transform, augmented by approximations whose accuracy guarantees are independent of $N$. Second, we develop a quantum spectral solver for regular linear ordinary differential equations based on the QUT. Under suitable boundary conditions and data-access assumptions, preconditioning keeps condition numbers bounded independently of the basis size, allowing the solution state to be prepared at polylogarithmic cost in system size and inverse error. Together, these contributions provide a framework for quantum spectral methods with the potential to solve linear differential equations efficiently.

title: Flux Crosstalk Calibration from Zero Knowledge to High Precision in Fully Tunable Superconducting Circuits
summary: Precise and independent flux control is essential for scalable superconducting processors built from frequency-tunable qubits and couplers, but flux crosstalk undermines it. Conventional calibration methods rely either on dedicated readout channels, which tunable couplers typically lack, or on readout schemes requiring extensive prior spectroscopy of the qubit and coupler. We demonstrate two independent methods that characterize coupler flux crosstalk without directly driving or measuring the couplers. The first method is zero-knowledge characterization, which exploits intrinsic coupler-resonator coupling to yield rapid and accurate estimates with no prior qubit or coupler spectroscopy, accelerating large scale bring-up. The second method is symmetric branch cancellation, which isolates crosstalk from other dispersive effects allowing for quantifying with high precision. Combined with an improved iterative procedure, these methods suppress residual coupler crosstalk below $5\times10^{-5}$, providing a complete route from zero-knowledge initialization to high-precision crosstalk characterization in fully tunable architectures.

title: Experimental activation of hidden metrological steerability in quantum channels via stochastic filtering
summary: Quantum steering-assisted metrology allows a trusted party (Bob) to improve local phase estimation by exploiting classical information communicated by an untrusted party (Alice). In realistic scenarios, however, the channel is subject to noise that degrades steerability and suppresses the associated metrological advantage. Here, we demonstrate that stochastic pre- and post-filtering operations can revive the violation of the metrological steering inequality (MSI) in phase-covariant amplitude-damping channels where it is initially absent, thereby activating a hidden metrological steerability and restoring their usefulness for quantum metrology. Specifically, the critical damping parameter beyond which the MSI violation is suppressed is raised from $γ_c \approx 0.5$ to $γ_c \approx 0.75$ for the largest filter strength considered. We verify this in a photonic experiment, where polarization qubits carrying the encoded phase are transmitted through an amplitude-damping channel implemented with a two-path Sagnac interferometer, and the stochastic operations are realized with glass plates at the Brewster angle. By tuning the filter strength and scanning the damping parameter over its full range, we observe the revival of the MSI violation, obtained at the cost of a reduced success probability inherent to the stochastic nature of the filtering operations. Our results establish that metrological utility and steerability can be activated through stochastic operations even when these properties are absent in the original noisy channel, extending filtering-based activation from witnesses of nonclassicality to a certified and operationally quantified metrological advantage.

title: QASPA-MaxCut on Unweighted Graphs: Edge Encoding and QAOA Restarts
summary: Max-Cut is a common testbed for near-term quantum optimization because it has a simple Ising Hamiltonian, established classical baselines, and a parameterized quantum circuit whose performance depends on the outer classical optimizer. This paper develops QASPA-MaxCut, a shift-phase circuit for Max-Cut that encodes graph edges through controlled $R_y$ rotations of the form $\mathrm{CX}_{ij}R_y(θ_{ij})\mathrm{CX}_{ij}$. We derive the exact two-qubit algebra of the edge block, trace an unweighted four-vertex example, and compare one-layer QASPA-MaxCut with depth-one QAOA by exact state-vector simulation. The protocol uses seed 42, evaluates connected backbone-augmented random graphs with additional-edge probabilities $p_{\mathrm{edge}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}$, and adds nineteen custom unweighted topologies. The QASPA-MaxCut score is reported after the algorithm's classical selection stage: the four leading QASPA bit strings are evaluated by the Max-Cut objective, and the best cut is retained. The QAOA score is the expected approximation ratio after local optimization, reported as a best-of-$k$ curve over one to ten restarts. In these small exact simulations, fixed-angle QASPA-MaxCut produces reported group-mean selection ratios between $0.955$ and $1.000$, the topology-level readout is unchanged in the retained finite-shot checks under the rule $\lceil 0.03047\cdot 2^n+1016.2\rceil$, and depth-one QAOA improves with additional classical restarts while remaining lower than the QASPA selection score in the reported mean summaries. This comparison motivates further study of the classical search budget needed to obtain competitive Max-Cut samples at shallow circuit depth.

title: Phase-Locked Quantum Battery Charging via Dissipative Mode Selection
summary: We investigate how dynamical instability and reservoir engineering can be harnessed to enhance the quality of quantum-battery charging in a bosonic two-mode system. We show that reservoir-engineered dissipative coupling selectively amplifies a single unstable quasi-dark mode, enabling phase-locked exponential charging at a reduced gain threshold, whereas coherent coupling can amplify two frequency-split unstable modes, resulting in persistent beating. This dissipative mode selection yields a near-unit ergotropy fraction and a substantially higher work-like signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), defined as ergotropy divided by the standard deviation of battery energy. Although optimizing the driving frequency enables coherent coupling to achieve faster charging and higher ergotropy power, dissipative coupling retains its advantage in the work-like SNR. An exact finite-time source-noise relation reveals that this advantage arises from a more constructive accumulation of coherent driving relative to incoherent fluctuations. Our results establish dissipative mode selection as a promising route to high-quality quantum-battery charging.

title: Solving a non-abelian hidden subgroup problem on a trapped-ion quantum computer: the power of the measurement basis
comment: 7 pages + 4-page appendix, 10 figures (6 in main text), 2 tables
summary: The hidden subgroup problem (HSP) unifies many of the best-known quantum speed-ups. For abelian groups it is solved efficiently by weak Fourier sampling, but for non-abelian groups, which include the cases relevant to graph isomorphism and lattice-based cryptography, the right measurement basis is crucial and often unknown. We experimentally study the HSP over the $q$-hedral groups $\mathbb{Z}_q \ltimes \mathbb{Z}_p$, which interpolate between the dihedral and affine groups and mark a boundary between instances that are efficiently solvable and those that are only information-theoretically solvable. On the IonQ Forte trapped-ion quantum computer, with $p \le 7$, we implement weak Fourier sampling, strong Fourier sampling in an adapted basis, strong Fourier sampling of adjacent pairs, and forgetful abelian sampling. We demonstrate that the theoretical predictions of Moore, Rockmore, Russell and Schulman survive on a noisy device: weak sampling reveals nothing about the hidden subgroup, the adapted basis succeeds for large $q$, adjacent pairs succeed for small $q$, and forgetful sampling saturates below unit success. For $p=7$, $q=6$, the hardware exceeds the success probability of an exhaustively optimised classical algorithm for up to three oracle queries.

title: A Quantum Lower Bound for Triangle Finding
summary:
Triangle finding is a fundamental problem in graph theory that has played a central role in the development of quantum algorithmic techniques. For $N$-vertex graphs given by their adjacency matrices, a long line of work has improved the quantum query upper bound from $O(N^{3/2})$ to $O(N^{5/4})$. However, the best known lower bound has remained the elementary $Ω(N)$ bound obtained from unstructured search. We prove the first superlinear quantum query lower bound for triangle finding, showing that $Ω(N^{13/12})$ queries are necessary. Our result also implies the same lower bound for triangle detection and for detecting every fixed connected non-bipartite graph.
  The proof builds on the compressed oracle approach of Zhandry and the transfer approaches of Belovs. It compares the computation on graphs with a planted triangle to the computation on random graphs conditioned to be triangle-free, through a map on the input registers that almost commutes with every query. We average over local changes to the input while preserving its distribution, through a procedure known as conditional resampling. Our main technical contribution is a set of estimates that let us control the query error under this averaging, despite the dependence introduced by conditioning a dense graph to be triangle-free.

title: Near-Quantum-Limited Readout for the Princeton Axion Search using a sub-GHz Kinetic Inductance Traveling Wave Parametric Amplifier
summary: Parametric amplifiers are a workhorse for near-quantum-limited measurements above 1 GHz. However, amplifier development has been more limited below 1 GHz. We present a kinetic inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifier (KI-TWPA) operating over 300-700 MHz, with gain exceeding 30 dB and pump powers of a few hundred nanowatts. The system noise performance, as measured by a variable-temperature noise source, is 2.5-3.5 quanta. This device is a versatile new tool for precision measurements of sub-GHz signals, with applications including readout of semiconductor spin qubits, superconducting detector arrays, and searches for new physics beyond the Standard Model. We characterize aspects of the amplifier performance relevant to axion searches, including gain drift, compression point, amplifier noise at various operating temperatures, readout with an input circulator, and magnetic field insensitivity.

title: Non-compact Kogut-Susskind gauge theories: 1D lattice models with exact ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ gauge invariance
summary: The Kogut-Susskind (KS) formulation of gauge theories constructs quantum many-body Hamiltonians with gauge invariance under a compact Lie group exactly implemented on a spatial lattice. Here, we revisit this construction for a non-compact gauge group. Although motivated in part by theories like general relativity whose first-order formulation involves the non-compact Lorentz group as a local symmetry, we focus on simpler cases in one spatial dimension akin to the Schwinger model. In a bottom-up approach, we show how exact gauge invariance under the simplest non-compact Lie group ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ can be retained exactly on a 1D lattice, and highlight the differences that arise with respect to compact gauge groups, including a continuous spectrum of the Casimir operators of the gauge fields and the emergence of infinite-dimensional representations of the matter fields. For the pure gauge theory, we discuss how a consistent restriction to the positive semigroup ${\rm SL}^{+}(2,\mathbb{R})$ reproduces well-known results from the quantization of Jackiw-Teitelboim (JT) gravity. Motivated by the constraint structure of general dilaton gravity, we introduce static charges coupled to the non-compact gauge field, which can be realised by single-fermion degrees of freedom living in an additional, synthetic dimension. With static charges our lattice model remains exactly integrable, but when extending to dynamical fermionic matter, we arrive at an interacting 1D ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ KS gauge theory. We give an interpretation of this model as a chain of charges sequentially connected by strings whose tension pulls matter left or right depending on the sign of the relative continuous ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ fluxes. This picture becomes exact when the involved ${\rm SL}(2,\mathbb{R})$ charges are strongly self-interacting, where we solve the reduced two-body problem analytically.

title: Entanglement Entropy in Non Relativistic Collisions
summary: We study numerically the build-up of entanglement entropy between two colliding, non relativistic particles, that are driven by the plain Schrödinger equation containing local, finite range potentials, and whose initial state is the product of two independent wave packets. Different situations are considered, ranging from a tunnel and mirror effect at low energy in front of a barrier, to higher energies, and also attraction rather than repulsion. While the calculated wave functions and density matrices significantly depend on the physical situations described by our models, the build-up trends and values in time of entanglement entropy look surprisingly alike one another.

title: Resource-efficient formulations of the Knapsack problem for quantum computing
summary: Quantum computing has emerged as a new tool for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Quantum optimization approaches usually operate on the subclass of Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems. Many optimization problems can be reformulated in this form, though there are often multiple ways to do so. The choice of formulation can considerably affect the performance of QUBO solvers in practice. In this work, we study QUBO formulations of the Knapsack problem, a canonical example of a problem with inequality constraints. In the standard formulation these constraints are converted into penalty terms, which requires additional slack variables. Here, we investigate three more resource-efficient approaches for formulating the Knapsack as a QUBO. The first two modify the standard formulation, either by deriving a smaller penalty constant or by reducing the number of slack variables. The third approach is a wholly different method, which avoids the use of slack variables entirely. All three approaches increase the probability of finding the optimal solution, both in simulations of the linear ramp Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (LR-QAOA) and on a D-Wave quantum annealer. The slackless method performs best, increasing success probabilities by several orders of magnitude even for relatively small problem sizes.

title: Finite-temperature transition-window weights on a fault-tolerant quantum computer: duplex filtering on a thermal purification
summary: The excite-filter-readout framework of Kharazi et al. computes zero-temperature response windows on a fault-tolerant quantum computer from a pure ground state. We extend it to Gibbs states, where the two objects decouple: filters act on absolute energies, a thermal response on transition frequencies. The extension rests on a Liouville-space/TFD identity, explicit in the block-encoding/QSP setting: the thermally weighted transition-window weight is a spectral projection of H_0 (x) I - I (x) H_0^T onto the Schmidt (thermofield-double) purification, instance of Rall's framework. Around it we assemble a routed-SELECT block encoding (one Hamiltonian query per filter query), a conjugate-pair readout, and a four-route (duplex, bin, Fourier-LCU, METTS) compatibility analysis. The cost is multiplicative and conditional: a per-window query bound M_"AE" * (2*sqrt(d/Z_"lb")*d_"vt" + 4*d_W), with a tight signal-adaptive count, the optimal sqrt(alpha beta) degree, and a window-edge term. The preparation factor sqrt(d/Z) grows exponentially with system size at fixed temperature in positive-entropy-density systems (2.08 -> 25.7, N = 8 to 14 at beta = 2), relieved only as beta -> 0. Zero temperature is recovered for beta G >= ln(2(d-1)||D||^2/epsilon). Identities are cross-checked between independent formula paths to 10^(-16)-10^(-12) and the readout assembly is validated at matrix level under a block-encoding promise.

title: Linear-time erasure recovery for quantum expander codes
summary: Erasures are used to model faults at a subset of known locations in various platforms used to construct fault-tolerant quantum computers. Beyond the utility in erasure recovery, efficient decoders for erasures are useful to both understand error decoders and as a subroutine for error decoding. Classical expander codes, which belong to the family of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, can be equipped with the Peeling decoder which works in linear time. Our main result is the algorithm Small-Set-Peeling, a quantum generalization of the classical Peeling decoder for erasures, that applies to quantum expander codes (Tillich, Zémor, IEEE T-IT 2013; Leverrier, Tillich, Zémor, FOCS 2015). This decoder can correct up to $D-1$ erasures, where $D$ is the (design) distance of the code and, importantly, is the first decoder that is guaranteed to do so in linear time. Combining with the erasure-conversion algorithm Small-Set-Find (Krishna, Livni-Navon, Wootters, SODA 2024), our result also implies the existence of a novel graph-local linear-time decoder for Pauli errors.

title: GFlowQEC: Generative Flow Networks that Learn to Sample Quantum LDPC Codes
summary: Choosing a quantum error-correcting code for a real device means scoring candidates with circuit-level simulations so slow that only a few hundred can be run. So every evaluation counts, and a search is judged by how many good codes it finds per paid evaluation. Quantum LDPC codes built from a few group elements protect many logical qubits, but good ones are rare in a huge space. We introduce GFlowQEC, to our knowledge the first generative flow network (GFlowNet) for quantum code design. It builds a code one group element at a time and learns to propose codes in proportion to a power of their score. We train it once on scores from earlier searches, freeze it, and let it propose lifted-product codes with 180 physical qubits, scored by their distances. Ranking ten of its draws per paid call, it finds more than twice as many new top-scoring codes (inequivalent to any it was trained on) as tuned parallel tempering, even when tempering starts from GFlowQEC's training codes. It finds more than three and a half times as many as a supervised screen ranking ten random candidates per call. When both rank a hundred, the screen beats GFlowQEC, and does best ranking GFlowQEC's draws. Soft Q-learning, which shares the GFlowNet's optimal policy, does as well at one noise bias and better at the other, so the gain does not depend on the GFlowNet's training loss. Trained proposers can make a budget of expensive evaluations go further when good codes are rare.

title: Quantum Algorithms for Molecular Response Functions: Resolvent Kernels, Time-Domain Sampling, Query Lower Bounds with Matched Single-Point Calibers, and a Six-Route Comparison
summary: Quantum algorithms for molecular response functions have mostly been studied one route at a time, most prominently the indicator-binning algorithm of Kharazi et al. We compare six routes within one accounting framework and state the conversions between their resource calibers. On the resolvent route the Lorentz-broadened spectrum is exactly a resolvent expectation; at finite gamma two boundary terms, a reversal term and a permanent-dipole pseudo-line, enter a disjoint error budget. Because the kernel subnormalization is exactly 1, the published binning accounting carries a removable Theta(alpha+1+omega) factor (49.69x and 7.75x at the definitional caliber), a correction that applies to both routes. Estimating the square root of the kernel amplitude lowers the readout cost from beta^2/mu_tilde_2 to beta/sqrt(mu_tilde_2). On the time-domain route we prove a single-point amplitude-estimation theorem and convert the generalized QPE of Loaiza et al. to the same accounting. The lower bounds are Theta_tilde(1/gamma) for parameter location, Theta(1/(gamma epsilon)) for windowed values, Omega(n/gamma) inside a restricted correlation-sampling class, and Omega(1/(epsilon gamma^2)) on the Lorentzian object; in the single-circuit-resolution caliber, gamma^(-n) is a grid-coverage artifact. Six routes, their calibers, an n=2 assembly with a component-grade coherence, and a phase diagram over the tested ensembles form one accounting map.

title: Optimal Holding Times for Entanglement Swapping
summary: We revisit the optimization of entanglement holding times in memory-based quantum repeaters for maximizing entanglement swapping throughput under different fidelity constraints - strict, probabilistic, and mean. We consider two heterogeneous quantum links that are equipped with single or multiple memories and differ in decoherence rates, memory capacities, entanglement attempt rates and success probabilities, as well as classical communication latencies. Efficient models are developed to estimate the expected entanglement throughput and the probability density functions of the conditional wait time to swap. The models are then used to satisfy different fidelity requirements by optimizing the maximum holding times for the two links. Finally, our proposed model and approach are validated with a discrete-event quantum network simulator.

title: Probing gravity at megahertz frequencies with levitated rotors
summary: The near-field gravitational interaction between masses is always thought of as instantaneous, an assumption experimentally tested only up to 1.7 kHz, where measurements yield a bounds at the $10^{-5}$ s level. We propose a near-field experiment reaching up to megahertz frequencies, in which a levitated microrotor modulates a mass quadrupole and a second rotor measures the resulting gravitational tidal field as a torque. Because the detector rotor acts as a mechanical local oscillator, the megahertz signal is downconverted to a convenient band of a few hertz, and since at fixed geometry neither the torque nor the integration time depends on the rotation rate, higher frequencies are reached at no cost in sensitivity. With parameters within reach of magnetically levitated NdFeB rotors, a signal at 2 MHz yields a torque of $2\cdot 10^{-25}$ Nm, detectable in under an hour at 10 mK. Treating a possible departure from instantaneous gravitational coupling through a field relaxation time, the measured torque could constrain it at the $10^{-8}$ s level, improving on the existing bounds by more than three orders of magnitude. As a byproduct of our analysis, we derive the sensitivity of a rotor operated as a tunable high-frequency gravitational-wave detector, finding that a noise-equivalent strain around $10^{-22}$ Hz$^{-1/2}$ could be achievable in the megahertz band.

title: Arithmetic Depth, Minimal Gate Alphabets, and Exact Program-State Resources for Single-Qubit Dyadic Programs
summary: Resource analyses for quantum programs commonly provide safe upper bounds on qubits, gates, or non-Clifford operations. We study a single-qubit dyadic fragment in which the deepest exact resource layer can instead be inferred exactly. Starting from the normalized-midpoint misty-state syntax, we define dyadic program states and the real cyclotomic tower $K_D=\mathbb Q(2\cos(π/2^D))$. For the projective single-qubit Clifford-cyclotomic tower $\widehat G_D\subseteq SO(3)$, we prove the relative intersection law $\widehat G_D\cap SO(3,K_d)=\widehat G_d$ for $d\le D$. Combining this descent theorem with an arithmetic-closure invariant for adaptive stabilizer processing yields $\mathrm{Fdepth}(U)=\mathrm{Adepth}(U)=\mathrm{Rdepth}(U)$: the smallest real cyclotomic field containing the Bloch matrix of an exactly synthesizable channel, the shallowest dyadic gate alphabet realizing it up to global phase, and the shallowest dyadic program-state layer sufficient for exact stabilizer-assisted implementation coincide. At that common minimum, known fixed-alphabet synthesis gives minimum primitive-rotation count. We package the result as an exact static resource effect and outline a certificate-producing compiler.

title: Using topology to reveal all mutually unbiased bases in dimension six
summary: Mutually unbiased bases (MUBs) describe complementary quantum measurements: certainty in one basis gives no information about the others.
